title: The networking VP (introduce yourself and your career)
power_dynamic: senior external stranger, warm but time-scarce and easily bored. Skims, drifts off if you ramble, rewards a crisp hook with genuine curiosity. No coaching, no rank moves.

text: I don't think we've met. What do you do?
Hey! Oh yeah, sure! Oh, I build products that make the internet and digital experience fun and live again.
That sounds like a heavy lift. What are you actually shipping right now?

People have been saying that, with so much exposure and time spent across screens and digital interfaces, there is a lack of going back to doing things in real life. There is that experience, that change, and shift. There are too many badly written, bad experiences, whether it's work or otherwise. The times have changed, expectations are much less, and the quality and ability to write good software have now come up. Thanks for the loans.
Not sure about the loans part. What are you actually building today?
Ah, LLMs. That makes more sense than bank loans. So what are you actually building with them?

I'm reimagining what practicing the learning pedagogy changes:
- the interface
- the value delivery
- the interaction
- the faster time to an aha moment
- the experience
Something that makes you feel like you're using more Wispr Flow for voice-to-speech and speech-to-text dictation for the first time. A similar, immersive experience and value through tough conversations, voice conversation, and product
You lost me on pedagogy a bit. Is it an app for roleplaying hard talks using voice?
Being put on the spot for tough conversations, more familiar and easy
Ah, a simulator for awkward talks. Who actually pays for that, HR teams or people practicing for Thanksgiving?

I see that being in those situations more often. The way to do this has always been to practice. For speeches, people do practice in front of the mirror, and they say it aloud at different times. There are so many such scenarios and situations, and the way the work happens is more icy, less collaborative, and less in person. In those rare moments, opportunities are few and real, and impressions are what's important and at stake. Practice makes things better, so why not?
Got it. So who actually pays?

My own struggles, I would say, are always about this: if you also have this situation where, post-conversation, on the same day or days later, you are like, “Oh, I should have said that instead of this, and it would have been so much better.” You keep feeling that sort of pain, and then you know you are the person for this.
Got it, the post-meeting regret is real. So who's actually opening their wallet for this?

It's an app with a voice. You have real human-like voice conversations around certain topics, themes, and areas of interest, which puts you in different simulated scenario situations close to that. You get guided. It's a two-way conversation, or something you say, record, and modulate. Look for the pace before it is saved and drive you on the pressure and help evaluate along the way.
Sounds neat. Still curious though, is this something individuals buy, or are you selling to enterprise learning teams?
